summary: Describes TCP SYN flooding attacks, which were well known at the time, and the various countermeasures with their tradeoffs. It archives explanations of the attack and common defenses for implementers and administrators, without making standards-level recommendations. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A SYN flood sends many connection requests that do not complete, using up a TCP server's space for pending connections. This RFC explains how the attack works and compares common ways to limit its effect.

questions: what is a tcp syn flood
how to mitigate syn flooding attacks
subtitle: How TCP SYN floods use half-open connections and what common defenses trade off

tldr.problem: A TCP server can retain state while it waits for a connection handshake to finish. An attacker can fill the server's limited queue with half-open connections and prevent new connections from being established.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes filtering, queue and timeout changes, SYN caches, SYN cookies, hybrid methods, and firewalls or proxies that handle the handshake.
tldr.outcome: It documents attack and mitigation techniques for implementers and administrators; it does not make standards-level recommendations or define one defense.

today: RFC 4987 is Informational, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It documents common SYN flood mitigations but does not make standards-level recommendations.

sections.title: How a SYN Flood Uses Server State
sections.content:
When a TCP server receives a SYN for a listening port, it begins keeping state for a connection while it waits for the rest of the handshake. Implementations limit how many such half-open connections they retain, often through a backlog associated with the listening application.

A SYN flood sends enough requests that do not complete to fill that backlog. The server may then ignore or replace connection requests, so legitimate clients cannot establish new connections. This RFC focuses on denial of service against a server or service, not attacks that exhaust the network's packet-processing capacity.
sections.plainLanguage: A server saves information while it waits for a new TCP connection to finish opening. A flood of requests that never finish can use up that space and prevent other connections from starting.

sections.title: What Makes the Attack Work
sections.content:
The attack depends on the size of the backlog, how quickly incomplete connection state expires, and whether the source addresses respond to the server's replies. Spoofed addresses that do not send a reset keep the server waiting; if real hosts receive the SYN-ACK, they can send resets that free the state.

The attacker must send new SYNs fast enough to replace state that the server reclaims. A group of compromised hosts can also produce the traffic, provided they suppress normal replies to SYN-ACKs. The attack targets new incoming connections to the affected listening service; the RFC says it does not, by itself, affect established connections or outgoing requests.
sections.plainLanguage: The server's queue fills when incomplete requests arrive faster than their saved state expires. Fake or controlled source hosts must avoid replying in a way that frees those entries.

sections.title: Filtering, SYN Cache and SYN Cookies
sections.content:
Filtering source-address spoofing can help, but the RFC says end hosts cannot assume such filtering is deployed everywhere. Increasing the backlog or shortening the wait can have performance or compatibility costs and may not stop an attacker who adjusts the traffic rate.

A SYN cache stores less information for an incomplete connection and allocates the full connection state after the handshake completes. SYN cookies allocate no per-connection state for the initial SYN; instead, the server encodes information in its SYN-ACK sequence number and reconstructs state if a valid ACK returns. Cookies can limit negotiation of some TCP options. Firewalls and proxies can also complete handshakes before passing connections to a protected server, shifting the burden to those devices.
sections.plainLanguage: Some defenses reduce how much state the server saves before a handshake finishes. A SYN cache saves a smaller record; a SYN cookie encodes needed information in a reply and reconstructs it if the client answers.

sections.title: Choosing a Mitigation
sections.content:
The RFC compares trade-offs rather than naming a universal solution. A SYN cache uses more memory than a cookie but avoids some option-negotiation limits. A cookie uses less memory, but the cookie scheme may not preserve all TCP options unless it has a way to encode them. Hybrid techniques can combine the cache and cookie approaches.

Firewalls and proxies can reduce the load on a server but move the problem and may change TCP's expected end-to-end behavior. The analysis says TCP implementations should provide some end-host defense because network filtering cannot be assumed. The document describes these as existing techniques and does not standardize them.
sections.plainLanguage: Each defense moves costs to a different place, such as memory, TCP option support or a firewall. The RFC documents these trade-offs so implementers and operators can assess them.

sections.title: Status and Security Context
sections.content:
The RFC says the attack and exploit tools were already publicly known when it was published. It presents countermeasures to help TCP implementers and server or network administrators understand how common defenses work and what side effects they may have.

The document does not define a standard defense. It excludes high-rate attacks aimed at the capacity of the network rather than the state of a TCP server.
sections.plainLanguage: This Informational RFC explains a known attack and defenses without changing TCP standards. It focuses on connection setup at a server, not on flooding a network's links or packet-processing capacity.
